title: Brothers and sisters
tomorrow: the little boy next door climbs on Amira's back mid-prayer. now what?

segments.voice: Yesterday, the middle door: a parent, close by and easy to walk past. Today, the people who came through the same door as you.

A photo memory pops up without asking: two young men grinning in front of a shop on its opening day. Brothers. And one of them hasn't called the other in years. Why don't they talk? Sometimes nobody can say exactly. A loan, a word at a wedding, a silence that got comfortable. So, one question for today: when a family tie goes quiet, what does it still ask of you?
screen: `TWO BROTHERS, ONE PHOTO.` → `A SILENCE THAT GOT COMFORTABLE.` → `WHAT DOES THE TIE STILL ASK?`

segments.voice: The Qur'an's answer starts further back than any family. In Pickthall's words: "O mankind! Be careful of your duty to your Lord Who created you from a single soul and from it created its mate and from them twain hath spread abroad a multitude of men and women." One soul at the root of everyone. Then the same verse names two things to guard: your duty to God, and the wombs that bore you. In Arabic the ties of kin are the rahim, the womb: the people who came from the same place you did. A hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari hangs that word on God's own name, al-Rahman, the Merciful. God says to it: whoever keeps you, I keep; whoever cuts you, I cut. So the tie isn't a feeling to wait for. It's a thing you keep, like a promise. Now a neighbor. The Psalms, read by Jews and Christians, sing about this too. In the King James Bible: "Behold, how good and how pleasant it is for brethren to dwell together in unity!" The same hope: siblings at one table. And one honest difference. The psalm sings how sweet unity is when it's there. The Qur'an and the hadith make keeping the tie a duty owed to God, even when it isn't sweet at all. One to tell a friend tonight: a single verse holds the whole human race and the brother down the hall.
screen: `FROM A SINGLE SOUL.` · `RAHIM: THE WOMB, THE TIE.` · `WHOEVER KEEPS IT, GOD KEEPS.` · `A PSALM: BRETHREN IN UNITY.` · then, large: `KEEP THE TIE.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind a brother, a sister, a cousin, any kin you've drifted from, or one you simply haven't called. On paper or in your notes, write one first line you could send them someday, plain and small. You don't have to send it; for now, just sit with it written.

segments.voice: Brothers and sisters: kin, the rahim, the ones who came from the same place. In the hadith, the tie hangs on God's own name.
Something to keep: keep the tie, even while it's quiet; one soul sits at the root of all of us. Three of ten, done.

howItsDone: Muslims call it silat al-rahim, keeping the ties of kin: visiting relatives, calling them and greeting them at Eid all count, and cutting family off is treated as a serious wrong.
